what_its_for: Anastrozole is used to treat breast cancer in women who have gone through menopause. It works by lowering the amount of estrogen your body makes, which can help slow or stop the growth of certain types of breast cancer that need estrogen to grow.
how_to_take: Take anastrozole by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day so it becomes part of your routine. Do not crush or chew the tablet.
dosing: The usual dose is one 1 mg tablet taken by mouth once a day. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed. Do not take more or less than your doctor tells you to.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next regular dose at the usual time. Never take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store anastrozole at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired tablets safely — ask your pharmacist how.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking tamoxifen or estrogen-containing products (such as hormone replacement therapy, estrogen creams, or birth control pills with estrogen) while taking anastrozole, as they can make this medicine less effective. Avoid alcohol in large amounts, as it may increase your risk of bone loss. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before starting any new medicines, supplements, or herbal products.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you have: severe bone, joint, or muscle pain; signs of a broken bone; chest pain or shortness of breath (possible signs of a blood clot); swelling, redness, or pain in your leg; numbness or weakness on one side of your body; sudden severe headache or vision changes; severe skin rash or blistering; unusual vaginal bleeding; or signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain. Also talk to your doctor if you feel very depressed or have significant mood changes.
when_it_works: Anastrozole starts lowering your estrogen levels within a few days of starting treatment. However, it may take several weeks to months before you or your doctor can tell if the medicine is helping with your cancer. Continue taking it even if you feel well, as this medicine works over a long period of time. Most people take it for at least 5 years.
special_populations: Older adults: No dose adjustment is usually needed, but older patients may be at higher risk for bone loss (osteoporosis) and should discuss bone health with their doctor. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, as this may affect how the medicine works in your body. Premenopausal women: Anastrozole is NOT recommended for women who have not yet gone through menopause, as it does not work the same way in this group. Pregnancy: Do not take anastrozole if you are pregnant or could become pregnant — it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Use effective non-hormonal birth control if needed. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine.
